2.1.200: Peace, lady! pause, or be more temperate:

2.1.219: All preparation for a bloody siege

2.1.233: And now, instead of bullets wrapp’d in fire,
2.1.234: To make a shaking fever in your walls,
2.1.235: They shoot but calm words folded up in smoke,

2.1.238: And let us in, your king, whose labour’d spirits,

2.1.240: Crave harbourage within your city walls.
2.1.241: When I have said, make answer to us both.

2.1.243: Is most divinely vow’d upon the right
2.1.244: Of him it holds, stands young Plantagenet,
2.1.245: Son to the elder brother of this man,
2.1.246: And king o’er him and all that he enjoys:
2.1.247: For this down-trodden equity, we tread
2.1.248: In warlike march these greens before your town,

2.1.250: Than the constraint of hospitable zeal
2.1.251: In the relief of this oppressed child
2.1.253: To pay that duty which you truly owe
2.1.254: To that owes it, namely this young prince:
2.1.255: And then our arms, like to a muzzled bear,
2.1.256: Save in aspect, hath all offence seal’d up;

2.1.258: Against the invulnerable clouds of heaven;

2.1.266: Can hide you from our messengers of war,

2.1.268: Were harbour’d in their rude circumference.

2.1.272: And stalk in blood to our possession?

2.1.277: To him will we prove loyal: till that time
2.1.278: Have we ramm’d up our gates against the world.

2.1.280: And if not that, I bring you witnesses,
2.1.281: Twice fifteen thousand hearts of England’s breed,—

2.1.286: Stand in his face to contradict his claim.
2.1.287: Till you compound whose right is worthiest,
2.1.288: We for the worthiest hold the right from both.
2.1.289: Then God forgive the sin of all those souls
2.1.291: Before the dew of evening fall, shall fleet,

2.1.293: Amen, amen! Mount, chevaliers! to arms!

2.1.299: I would set an ox-head to your lion’s hide,
2.1.300: And make a monster of you.
2.1.302: O tremble, for you hear the lion roar.
2.1.303: Up higher to the plain; where we’ll set forth
2.1.304: In best appointment all our regiments.
2.1.305: Speed then, to take advantage of the field.
2.1.306: It shall be so; and at the other hill
2.1.307: Command the rest to stand. God and our right!
2.1.308: You men of Angiers, open wide your gates,
2.1.309: And let young Arthur, Duke of Bretagne, in,

2.1.311: Much work for tears in many an English mother,

2.1.330: Our lusty English, all with purpled hands,

2.1.332: Open your gates and gives the victors way.

2.1.337: Blood hath bought blood and blows have answered blows;

2.1.342: France, hast thou yet more blood to cast away?
2.1.343: Say, shall the current of our right run on?
2.1.344: Whose passage, vex’d with thy impediment,
2.1.345: Shall leave his native channel and o’erswell
2.1.346: With course disturb’d even thy confining shores,
2.1.347: Unless thou let his silver water keep
2.1.348: A peaceful progress to the ocean.
2.1.349: England, thou hast not saved one drop of blood,
2.1.350: In this hot trial, more than we of France;
2.1.351: Rather, lost more. And by this hand I swear,
2.1.352: That sways the earth this climate overlooks,
2.1.353: Before we will lay down our just-borne arms,
2.1.354: We’ll put thee down, ’gainst whom these arms we bear,
2.1.355: Or add a royal number to the dead,
2.1.356: Gracing the scroll that tells of this war’s loss
2.1.357: With slaughter coupled to the name of kings.
2.1.358: Ha, majesty! how high thy glory towers,
2.1.359: When the rich blood of kings is set on fire!
2.1.360: O, now doth Death line his dead chaps with steel;
2.1.361: The swords of soldiers are his teeth, his fangs;
2.1.362: And now he feasts, mousing the flesh of men,
2.1.364: Why stand these royal fronts amazed thus?
2.1.365: Cry, ‘havoc!’ kings; back to the stained field,
2.1.366: You equal potents, fiery kindled spirits!
2.1.367: Then let confusion of one part confirm
2.1.368: The other’s peace: till then, blows, blood and death!
2.1.369: Whose party do the townsmen yet admit?
2.1.370: Speak, citizens, for England; who’s your king?
2.1.371: The king of England; when we know the king.
2.1.372: Know him in us, that here hold up his right.
2.1.373: In us, that are our own great deputy
2.1.374: And bear possession of our person here,
2.1.375: Lord of our presence, Angiers, and of you.
2.1.376: A greater power then we denies all this;
2.1.377: And till it be undoubted, we do lock
2.1.378: Our former scruple in our strong-barr’d gates;
2.1.379: King’d of our fears, until our fears, resolved,
2.1.380: Be by some certain king purged and deposed.
2.1.381: By heaven, these scroyles of Angiers flout you, kings,
2.1.382: And stand securely on their battlements,
2.1.383: As in a theatre, whence they gape and point
2.1.384: At your industrious scenes and acts of death.
2.1.385: Your royal presences be ruled by me:
2.1.386: Do like the mutines of Jerusalem,
2.1.387: Be friends awhile and both conjointly bend
2.1.388: Your sharpest deeds of malice on this town:
2.1.389: By east and west let France and England mount
2.1.390: Their battering cannon charged to the mouths,
2.1.391: Till their soul-fearing clamours have brawl’d down
2.1.392: The flinty ribs of this contemptuous city:
2.1.393: I’ld play incessantly upon these jades,
2.1.395: Leave them as naked as the vulgar air.
2.1.396: That done, dissever your united strengths,
2.1.397: And part your mingled colours once again;
2.1.398: Turn face to face and bloody point to point;
2.1.399: Then, in a moment, Fortune shall cull forth
2.1.400: Out of one side her happy minion,
2.1.401: To whom in favour she shall give the day,
2.1.402: And kiss him with a glorious victory.
2.1.403: How like you this wild counsel, mighty states?
2.1.404: Smacks it not something of the policy?
2.1.405: Now, by the sky that hangs above our heads,
2.1.406: I like it well. France, shall we knit our powers
2.1.407: And lay this Angiers even to the ground;
2.1.408: Then after fight who shall be king of it?
2.1.409: An if thou hast the mettle of a king,
2.1.410: Being wronged as we are by this peevish town,
2.1.411: Turn thou the mouth of thy artillery,
2.1.412: As we will ours, against these saucy walls;
2.1.413: And when that we have dash’d them to the ground,
2.1.414: Why then defy each other and pell-mell
2.1.415: Make work upon ourselves, for heaven or hell.
2.1.416: Let it be so. Say, where will you assault?
2.1.417: We from the west will send destruction
2.1.421: Shall rain their drift of bullets on this town.
2.1.422: O prudent discipline! From north to south:
2.1.423: Austria and France shoot in each other’s mouth:
2.1.424: I’ll stir them to it. Come, away, away!
2.1.425: Hear us, great kings: vouchsafe awhile to stay,
2.1.426: And I shall show you peace and fair-faced league;
2.1.427: Win you this city without stroke or wound;
2.1.428: Rescue those breathing lives to die in beds,
2.1.429: That here come sacrifices for the field:
2.1.430: Persever not, but hear me, mighty kings.
2.1.431: Speak on with favour; we are bent to hear.
2.1.432: That daughter there of Spain, the Lady Blanch,
2.1.433: Is niece to England: look upon the years
2.1.434: Of Lewis the Dauphin and that lovely maid:
2.1.435: If lusty love should go in quest of beauty,
2.1.436: Where should he find it fairer than in Blanch?
2.1.437: If zealous love should go in search of virtue,
2.1.438: Where should he find it purer than in Blanch?
2.1.439: If love ambitious sought a match of birth,
2.1.440: Whose veins bound richer blood than Lady Blanch?
2.1.441: Such as she is, in beauty, virtue, birth,
2.1.442: Is the young Dauphin every way complete:
2.1.443: If not complete of, say he is not she;
2.1.444: And she again wants nothing, to name want,
2.1.445: If want it be not that she is not he:
2.1.446: He is the half part of a blessed man,
2.1.447: Left to be finished by such as she;
2.1.448: And she a fair divided excellence,
2.1.449: Whose fulness of perfection lies in him.
2.1.450: O, two such silver currents, when they join,
2.1.451: Do glorify the banks that bound them in;
2.1.452: And two such shores to two such streams made one,
2.1.453: Two such controlling bounds shall you be, kings,
2.1.454: To these two princes, if you marry them.
2.1.455: This union shall do more than battery can
2.1.456: To our fast-closed gates; for at this match,
2.1.457: With swifter spleen than powder can enforce,
2.1.458: The mouth of passage shall we fling wide ope,
2.1.459: And give you entrance: but without this match,
2.1.460: The sea enraged is not half so deaf,
2.1.461: Lions more confident, mountains and rocks
2.1.462: More free from motion, no, not Death himself
2.1.463: In moral fury half so peremptory,
2.1.464: As we to keep this city.
2.1.466: That shakes the rotten carcass of old Death
2.1.467: Out of his rags! Here’s a large mouth, indeed,
2.1.468: That spits forth death and mountains, rocks and seas,
2.1.469: Talks as familiarly of roaring lions
2.1.470: As maids of thirteen do of puppy-dogs!
2.1.471: What cannoneer begot this lusty blood?
2.1.472: He speaks plain cannon fire, and smoke and bounce;
2.1.473: He gives the bastinado with his tongue:
2.1.474: Our ears are cudgell’d; not a word of his
2.1.475: But buffets better than a fist of France:
2.1.476: Zounds! I was never so bethump’d with words
2.1.477: Since I first call’d my brother’s father dad.
2.1.478: Son, list to this conjunction, make this match;
2.1.479: Give with our niece a dowry large enough:
2.1.480: For by this knot thou shalt so surely tie
2.1.481: Thy now unsured assurance to the crown,
2.1.482: That yon green boy shall have no sun to ripe
2.1.483: The bloom that promiseth a mighty fruit.
2.1.484: I see a yielding in the looks of France;
2.1.485: Mark, how they whisper: urge them while their souls
2.1.487: Lest zeal, now melted by the windy breath
2.1.488: Of soft petitions, pity and remorse,
2.1.489: Cool and congeal again to what it was.
2.1.490: Why answer not the double majesties
2.1.491: This friendly treaty of our threaten’d town?
2.1.492: Speak England first, that hath been forward first
2.1.493: To speak unto this city: what say you?
2.1.494: If that the Dauphin there, thy princely son,
2.1.495: Can in this book of beauty read ‘I love,’
2.1.496: Her dowry shall weigh equal with a queen:
2.1.497: For Anjou and fair Touraine, Maine, Poictiers,
2.1.498: And all that we upon this side the sea,
2.1.499: Except this city now by us besieged,
2.1.500: Find liable to our crown and dignity,
2.1.501: Shall gild her bridal bed and make her rich
2.1.503: As she in beauty, education, blood,
2.1.504: Holds hand with any princess of the world.
2.1.505: What say’st thou, boy? look in the lady’s face.
2.1.506: I do, my lord; and in her eye I find
2.1.507: A wonder, or a wondrous miracle,
2.1.508: The shadow of myself form’d in her eye:
2.1.509: Which being but the shadow of your son,
2.1.510: Becomes a sun and makes your son a shadow:
2.1.511: I do protest I never loved myself
2.1.512: Till now infixed I beheld myself
2.1.513: Drawn in the flattering table of her eye.
2.1.514: Drawn in the flattering table of her eye!
2.1.515: Hang’d in the frowning wrinkle of her brow!
2.1.516: And quarter’d in her heart! he doth espy
2.1.517: Himself love’s traitor: this is pity now,
2.1.518: That hang’d and drawn and quartered, there should be
2.1.519: In such a love so vile a lout as he.
2.1.520: My uncle’s will in this respect is mine:
2.1.521: If he see aught in you that makes him like,
2.1.522: That any thing he sees, which moves his liking,
2.1.523: I can with ease translate it to my will;
2.1.524: Or if you will, to speak more properly,
2.1.525: I will enforce it easily to my love.
2.1.526: Further I will not flatter you, my lord,
2.1.527: That all I see in you is worthy love,
2.1.528: Than this; that nothing do I see in you,
2.1.529: Though churlish thoughts themselves should be your judge,
2.1.530: That I can find should merit any hate.
2.1.531: What say these young ones? What say you my niece?
2.1.532: That she is bound in honour still to do
2.1.533: What you in wisdom still vouchsafe to say.
2.1.534: Speak then, prince Dauphin; can you love this lady?
2.1.535: Nay, ask me if I can refrain from love;
2.1.536: For I do love her most unfeignedly.
2.1.537: Then do I give Volquessen, Touraine, Maine,
2.1.538: Poictiers and Anjou, these five provinces,
2.1.539: With her to thee; and this addition more,
2.1.540: Full thirty thousand marks of English coin.
2.1.541: Philip of France, if thou be pleased withal,
2.1.542: Command thy son and daughter to join hands.
2.1.543: It likes us well; young princes, close your hands.
2.1.544: And your lips too; for I am well assured
2.1.545: That I did so when I was first assured.
2.1.546: Now, citizens of Angiers, ope your gates,
2.1.547: Let in that amity which you have made;
2.1.548: For at Saint Mary’s chapel presently
2.1.549: The rites of marriage shall be solemnized.
2.1.550: Is not the Lady Constance in this troop?
2.1.551: I know she is not, for this match made up
2.1.552: Her presence would have interrupted much:
2.1.553: Where is she and her son? tell me, who knows.
2.1.554: She is sad and passionate at your highness’ tent.
2.1.555: And, by my faith, this league that we have made
2.1.556: Will give her sadness very little cure.
2.1.557: Brother of England, how may we content
2.1.558: This widow lady? In her right we came;
2.1.559: Which we, God knows, have turn’d another way,
2.1.562: For we’ll create young Arthur Duke of Bretagne
2.1.563: And Earl of Richmond; and this rich fair town
2.1.564: We make him lord of. Call the Lady Constance;
2.1.565: Some speedy messenger bid her repair
2.1.566: To our solemnity: I trust we shall,
2.1.567: If not fill up the measure of her will,
2.1.568: Yet in some measure satisfy her so
2.1.569: That we shall stop her exclamation.
2.1.570: Go we, as well as haste will suffer us,
2.1.571: To this unlook’d for, unprepared pomp.
2.1.572: Mad world! mad kings! mad composition!
2.1.573: John, to stop Arthur’s title in the whole,
2.1.574: Hath willingly departed with a part,
2.1.575: And France, whose armour conscience buckled on,
2.1.576: Whom zeal and charity brought to the field
2.1.577: As God’s own soldier, rounded in the ear
2.1.578: With that same purpose-changer, that sly devil,
2.1.579: That broker, that still breaks the pate of faith,
2.1.580: That daily break-vow, he that wins of all,
2.1.581: Of kings, of beggars, old men, young men, maids,
2.1.582: Who, having no external thing to lose
2.1.583: But the word ‘maid,’ cheats the poor maid of that,
2.1.585: Commodity, the bias of the world,
2.1.586: The world, who of itself is peised well,
2.1.587: Made to run even upon even ground,
2.1.588: Till this advantage, this vile-drawing bias,
2.1.589: This sway of motion, this Commodity,
2.1.590: Makes it take head from all indifferency,
2.1.591: From all direction, purpose, course, intent:
2.1.592: And this same bias, this Commodity,
2.1.593: This bawd, this broker, this all-changing word,
2.1.594: Clapp’d on the outward eye of fickle France,
2.1.595: Hath drawn him from his own determined aid,
2.1.596: From a resolved and honourable war,
2.1.597: To a most base and vile-concluded peace.
2.1.598: And why rail I on this Commodity?
2.1.599: But for because he hath not woo’d me yet:
2.1.600: Not that I have the power to clutch my hand,
2.1.601: When his fair angels would salute my palm;
2.1.602: But for my hand, as unattempted yet,
2.1.603: Like a poor beggar, raileth on the rich.
2.1.604: Well, whiles I am a beggar, I will rail
2.1.605: And say there is no sin but to be rich;
2.1.606: And being rich, my virtue then shall be
2.1.607: To say there is no vice but beggary.
2.1.608: Since kings break faith upon commodity,
2.1.609: Gain, be my lord, for I will worship thee.
3.1.1: Gone to be married! gone to swear a peace!
3.1.2: False blood to false blood join’d! gone to be friends!
3.1.3: Shall Lewis have Blanch, and Blanch those provinces?
3.1.4: It is not so; thou hast misspoke, misheard:
3.1.5: Be well advised, tell o’er thy tale again:
3.1.6: It cannot be; thou dost but say ’tis so:

3.1.8: Is but the vain breath of a common man:

3.1.12: For I am sick and capable of fears,
3.1.13: Oppress’d with wrongs and therefore full of fears,
3.1.14: A widow, husbandless, subject to fears,
3.1.15: A woman, naturally born to fears;

3.1.17: With my vex’d spirits I cannot take a truce,

3.1.20: Why dost thou look so sadly on my son?
3.1.21: What means that hand upon that breast of thine?
3.1.22: Why holds thine eye that lamentable rheum,
3.1.23: Like a proud river peering o’er his bounds?
3.1.24: Be these sad signs confirmers of thy words?
3.1.25: Then speak again; not all thy former tale,
3.1.26: But this one word, whether thy tale be true.
3.1.27: As true as I believe you think them false
3.1.28: That give you cause to prove my saying true.
3.1.29: O, if thou teach me to believe this sorrow,
3.1.30: Teach thou this sorrow how to make me die,
3.1.31: And let belief and life encounter so
3.1.32: As doth the fury of two desperate men
3.1.33: Which in the very meeting fall and die.
3.1.34: Lewis marry Blanch! O boy, then where art thou?
3.1.35: France friend with England, what becomes of me?
3.1.36: Fellow, be gone: I cannot brook thy sight:
3.1.37: This news hath made thee a most ugly man.
3.1.38: What other harm have I, good lady, done,
3.1.39: But spoke the harm that is by others done?
3.1.40: Which harm within itself so heinous is
3.1.41: As it makes harmful all that speak of it.
